transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-12-31 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 min
Attendees: Morgan (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Daniel (Cascade CTO), Priya (ML Eng), Ethan (Infra)

Summary:
Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on quantization profiles (INT8 vs FP8) and quality vs latency tradeoffs. Customer wants baseline latency targets ~50-120ms per request for 512 tokens, and is sensitive to quality regressions for their summarization pipeline. Discussed Redwood quant profiles, benchmark methodology, fallback/canary approaches, and next steps for pilot.

Topics:
- INT8 and FP8 quality differences on summarization and instruction-following tasks
- Latency/throughput numbers (p50/p95) and batching behavior
- How Redwood Optimize recommends profiles and auto-rollout/fallbacks
- Private/Dedicated considerations (KMS, VPC, SOC2 logs)

Transcript:
00:00 Morgan (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, happy new year early, we'll do a 45 to 50 minute walkthrough of Optimize quant profiles, i think the ask from Daniel was, right, how do int8 and fp8 behave on your workloads and what sorts of latency wins we can see without blowing up quality, correct?
00:12 Daniel (Cascade CTO): yep that's right, we run a lot of summarization and multi-turn chat for internal knowledge search. Latency's gotta be reasonable, ideally p95 under 200ms and p50 as low as possible for shorter responses. also, security is a must, we need to know about KMS and audit logs.
00:28 Sofia (Redwood SE): awesome, we'll go through our quant profiles, show some benchmark numbers, and then demo the Optimize console suggestions. a couple notes up front: int8 gets you the biggest cost/latency wins but can sometimes introduce small quality regressions on very sensitive instruction-following prompts; fp8 tends to be a sweet spot in many cases.
00:45 Priya (ML Eng): can you define what you mean by "profile" — is that a per-model config or per-route?
00:52 Sofia (Redwood SE): good question. a profile is essentially a set of parameters: quantization level (int8, fp8, bf16 fallback), per-layer exceptions, KV cache settings, per-token beam/temperature constraints, and runtime knobs like continuous batching window. profiles can be attached at model version level or per-route in the API, so you can run different profiles for different workloads.
01:20 Ethan (Infra): and how does that interact with dedicated vs hosted? we want to know about isolation and also about network  VPC peering or private link for hosted. KMS support for private deployment or dedicated with customer-managed keys. we'll share the security packet after.
01:45 Sofia (Redwood SE): jumping into numbers — caveat these are from our internal microbenchmarks on 8xA40-style instances, real numbers will vary. comparing baseline FP16 to FP8 and INT8 on a 7B-ish transformer for a 512 token generation: FP16 p50 ~180ms, p95 ~450ms; FP8 p50 ~120ms, p95 ~300ms; INT8 p50 ~90ms, p95 ~260ms. cost per token drops roughly 2x with INT8 vs FP16, fp8 is ~1.4x cost reduction.
02:10 Priya (ML Eng): those p95 numbers seem high for our targets, we generally expect shorter responses but our distribution is skewed — mostly 50–150 tokens. how do these scale with length?
02:22 Sofia (Redwood SE): good call. for 128 tokens the p50/p95 reduce by ~30–40% across the board — so INT8 p50 down to ~40–50ms in our tests. also continuous batching helps throughput but can add 10–40ms on tail depending on batching window. there's a tradeoff: increasing batching raises throughput and lowers cost per token but hurts tail latency.
02:48 Daniel (Cascade CTO): okay so is FP8 generally safer for quality? any examples of failure modes?
02:54 Sofia (Redwood SE): FP8 tends to preserve logits better in attention-heavy layers, so instruction-following and chain-of-thought can be safer. INT8 sometimes causes token-level artifacts: repetition, slight hallucination increases on edge prompts. but we provide per-layer exceptions — you can quantize most layers to INT8 but keep a few sensitive layers at FP16 or FP8.
03:15 Priya (ML Eng): do you have a recommended workflow to validate quality degradation? we run ROUGE / BLEU-ish metrics for summarization and also human evals.
03:24 Sofia (Redwood SE): we recommend a three-stage workflow: local evals (automated metrics on a holdout set), Redwood Optimize's quality regression checks where we run your eval set against candidate profiles and surface delta metrics, and a small A/B canary in production with automatic rollback thresholds. we'll demo the Optimize UI in a sec.
03:40 Morgan (Redwood AE): question for you — what's your tolerance on quality delta? like how many percentage points ROUGE or whatever is acceptable?
03:47 Daniel (Cascade CTO): we can tolerate up to 1.5% drift on our weighted summary score, after that product starts to complain.
03:52 Sofia (Redwood SE): perfect, that's helpful — Optimize's thresholds are configurable and we'll hook your metric.
04:05 (screen share starts, Optimize console)
04:20 Sofia (Redwood SE): here's the profile gallery — you can see predefined profiles: conservative-fp8, balanced-fp8-int8, aggressive-int8. each profile shows expected latency/throughput and approximate quality delta from our baseline. note these are estimates until we run your eval set.
04:45 Priya (ML Eng): what's the process to get per-customer calibrated estimates?
04:50 Sofia (Redwood SE): upload a small eval set (we usually ask 500–2k samples), we run batch inference across candidate profiles, compute your metrics (ROUGE, exact-match, perplexity), and produce plots: quality delta vs latency and cost. you can then choose per-route defaults and set auto-rollout policies.
05:10 Ethan (Infra): on the private/dedicated side, do you run those same Optimize jobs in our VPC? we can't send eval sets externally.
05:18 Morgan (Redwood AE): yes, for private deployments the Optimize runner can be deployed in customer environment (air-gapped option) or we can do an encrypted transfer under NDA. we'll capture audit logs and store them per your retention settings.
05:32 Daniel (Cascade CTO): curious about KV cache behavior you mentioned earlier — does quantization impact resuming and latency for multi-turn?
05:38 Sofia (Redwood SE): quantization affects the model weights not the KV cache directly, but reduced precision can change cache hit behavior slightly because of rounding; we observed small differences in warm-start latency. Optimize can recommend keeping higher precision for models with long multi-turn history or enabling hybrid caching.
05:55 Priya (ML Eng): can you show an example of a regression report?
06:00 Sofia (Redwood SE): sure, here's a sample run — baseline FP16 vs INT8: avg ROUGE drop 0.9%, some samples flagged with hallucinations; the UI highlights top failure cases with inputs and candidate outputs. you can filter by route or prompt type.
06:20 Daniel (Cascade CTO): do you tie this into alerts? we want to be notified if quality crosses threshold.
06:24 Sofia (Redwood SE): yes, Optimize can emit alerts to Slack, pager, or webhook when regression crosses configured thresholds, and optionally stop rollout and automatically rollback to the previous profile.
06:35 Morgan (Redwood AE): another practical note — quantization recompute time: when you change profiles, models might need to be recompiled on the runtime which can take 1–5 minutes depending on model size and infra. we surface those timings in the console.
06:50 Ethan (Infra): what's the expected memory footprint change for INT8 vs FP16?
06:55 Sofia (Redwood SE): INT8 can reduce GPU memory by ~2x which can allow higher batch sizes or more concurrent shards; fp8 is in between. that affects how many concurrent requests you can serve per GPU.
07:08 Priya (ML Eng): any known incompatibilities with certain model families — e.g., instruction-tuned Llama variants or newer transformer blocks?
07:15 Sofia (Redwood SE): some custom layers or exotic fused kernels sometimes need manual per-layer exceptions; we maintain a model catalog with verified profiles. for very new model families we'll run a quick compatibility job.
07:30 (15 min demo walk-through of UI, skipped in transcript for brevity)
22:45 Sofia (Redwood SE): jumping back to the benchmark CSV — i'll highlight the key columns: prompt_id, tokens_in, tokens_out, profile, p50_ms, p95_ms, avg_quality_metric. we also include raw logits checks for debugging.
23:05 Priya (ML Eng): do you provide the raw outputs for human annotation?
23:10 Sofia (Redwood SE): yes we export candidate outputs and diffs; many customers use that for small human-in-the-loop review sets.
23:25 Daniel (Cascade CTO): okay, let's talk pilot scope and success criteria — we want to validate on 1) latency p95 under 220ms for our 95th percentile of requests, 2) weighted summary metric delta < 1.5%, 3) no data exfiltration risks.
23:45 Morgan (Redwood AE): got it. proposed pilot: 2 weeks, run 50k requests across your most common routes, we'll run FP16 baseline then FP8 and INT8 candidate profiles; Optimize will produce the quality-vs-latency matrices and a recommended profile.
24:05 Ethan (Infra): network and key management — we need ability to use our KMS and logs to our SIEM.
24:12 Morgan (Redwood AE): supported — Dedicated and Private both allow customer-managed KMS; audit logs can stream to your SIEM via syslog or S3 with lifecycle policies.
24:25 Priya (ML Eng): how do you handle safety/regression if we detect hallucinations in INT8? is rollback instantaneous?
24:30 Sofia (Redwood SE): rollback is fast at the routing layer — traffic can be switched back to previous profile in under a minute; the model binary might still be warmed on other hosts but traffic control prevents exposure. plus you can set automatic rollback thresholds.
24:48 Daniel (Cascade CTO): any pricing delta for FP8 vs INT8?
24:52 Morgan (Redwood AE): pricing is usage-based; INT8 gives lower unit cost because of GPU utilization improvements. we'll include model-specific cost estimates in the spreadsheet — generally INT8 30–45% cheaper than FP16 depending on batch and sequence length; FP8 about 20–30% cheaper.
25:10 Priya (ML Eng): what about long-term model updates — if we push a new model version, do we need to re-run all profiles?
25:17 Sofia (Redwood SE): yes, model changes require re-evaluation. Optimize keeps versioned profiles and can run a regression job automatically on new model versions before rollout.
25:30 (Customer asks about competitors briefly)
25:35 Daniel (Cascade CTO): curious if you or competitors like NVIDIA or cloud providers do different quantization approaches that impact our choice?
25:44 Sofia (Redwood SE): NVIDIA has kernel-level optimizations and specific tools; cloud providers vary. Optimize's advantage is integrated profiling + per-route rollout + observability so you can tune in production with rollback.
26:00 (short silence, everyone reviewing slides)
26:15 Priya (ML Eng): okay practical question — what's the minimal eval set size you recommend to get reliable ROUGE deltas?
26:21 Sofia (Redwood SE): 500 samples gives a directional signal; 2k is preferred for stable stats. we also recommend stratifying by prompt type — e.g., summarization, instruction, chit-chat.
26:35 Daniel (Cascade CTO): timeline if we want to run the pilot in mid-Jan?
26:40 Morgan (Redwood AE): we can start setup early Jan, if you send the eval set and confirm infra constraints by Jan 6 we can kick off the pilot the week of Jan 11.
26:52 Ethan (Infra): which logs do you need from our side? we'll want minimal exposure.
26:58 Sofia (Redwood SE): we need request/response hashes not raw content by default, but for quality runs you can provide masked or anonymized content. for private deployments the runner can stay in your VPC and nothing leaves.
27:12 Priya (ML Eng): will you support per-prompt exceptions so some prompts keep FP16?
27:17 Sofia (Redwood SE): yes, per-route or per-prompt override is supported via route rules in the console.
27:25 Daniel (Cascade CTO): okay this looks promising. any final caveats?
27:30 Sofia (Redwood SE): main caveat is that results are workload dependent; the Optimize estimates are starting points. unusual model architectures or very long context windows may need custom tuning.
27:40 Morgan (Redwood AE): recap and next steps: we'll send the benchmark template and pricing, Sofia will send sample quant profiles and CLI commands, Cascade will prepare eval set and confirm KMS/VPC details.
27:55 Daniel (Cascade CTO): sounds good. thanks all, excited to try it.
28:00 Morgan (Redwood AE): great, we'll follow up with the mail and a calendar invite for pilot kickoff. thanks everyone.

(End meeting)
